title: Support Vector Machine
description: See how a support vector machine finds the widest street between two classes, which points hold it up, and how the kernel trick bends it. Free and interactive.
youWillLearn: Why the widest gap between classes is the safest boundary
What support vectors are and why only they matter
How C trades a wide street against mistakes
How the kernel trick draws curved boundaries

story.title: Many lines split them
story.body: Two groups of points, nicely apart. You could draw countless straight lines between them and every one would classify all points correctly. Which line should we trust for **new** points?
story.keyIdea: Getting the training points right isn't enough; we want the line that is safest for points we haven't seen.

story.title: Build the widest street
story.body: A support vector machine looks for the widest **street** that separates the groups: the solid blue line runs down the middle and the dashed lines are its edges. A wide street leaves room for new points that land a bit off from the old ones.
story.keyIdea: The best boundary is the one with the biggest margin to both groups.
story.math: The model is `f(x) = w·x + b`. The middle line is `f(x) = 0`, the edges are `f(x) = ±1`, and the street's width is `2 / |w|`, so a wide street means a small `w`.

story.title: Points push the street
story.body: Training visits the points in random order. A point that is safely outside the street does nothing. A point **inside the street or on the wrong side** pushes the boundary away from itself (orange halo). The strip on the right shows where every point stands: on the wrong side, in the street, or safe.
story.keyIdea: Only points that are too close or wrong ever change the model.
story.math: This is the Pegasos algorithm: for a picked point, if `y·f(x) < 1` then its push count `α` goes up by one. The street you see is the **average** of the street over all steps so far, which keeps it from jumping around.

story.title: Only a few points matter
story.body: The street's formula is a weighted sum over the circled points only: the **support vectors**, the points that pushed at some moment during training. At the exact SVM solution they would be precisely the points on the edges of the street or inside it. This quick training method gets close, so a few circled points pushed early on and have since been left behind.
story.keyIdea: The boundary is built from the support vectors; the other points never enter its formula.

story.title: How strict should it be?
story.body: Real data overlaps, so no street is perfectly clear. The setting **C** decides the trade-off. A small C accepts some points inside the street (or even on the wrong side) to keep it wide. A large C insists on fewer violations, so the street gets narrower to fit the points more strictly.
story.keyIdea: C balances a wide margin against training mistakes.
story.math: The SVM minimises `λ/2·|w|² + mean(max(0, 1 − y·f(x)))` with `λ = 1/(C·n)`: the first part wants a wide street, the second (the *hinge loss*) punishes points inside it.

story.title: Bending the street
story.body: What if no straight street exists, like one group inside a ring of the other? The **kernel trick** measures similarity in a smarter way, so the same algorithm draws curved streets. Try it in the Lab: pick **Rings**, then **Curved (RBF)**.
story.keyIdea: A kernel lets a linear method draw curved boundaries without ever computing new features.
story.math: Replace the dot product `xᵢ·x` with a kernel. The RBF kernel `K(a, b) = e^(−γ·|a − b|²)` says how close two points are; `γ` sets how far each point's influence reaches.

init.title: Start: no boundary yet
init.body: Every point will be visited once per epoch. Press play to start.

pick.title: Epoch {epoch}: who pushes?
pick.body: The highlighted points pushed the boundary at some moment during this epoch: they were inside the street or on the wrong side when they were visited.

update.title: Epoch {epoch}: the street moves
update.body: Accuracy {accuracy}; {inside} points are on or inside the street.

done.title: Done after {epoch} epochs
done.body: Fraction correct {accuracy}, built from {supports} support vectors. Try another C, or the curved kernel.

lab.breakIt: On **Overlapping**, slide **C** down to **0.01**: the street gets so wide that many points sit inside it and some end up on the wrong side. Push C to **100** and the street narrows to fit the points more strictly. Then pick **Rings** with **Curved (RBF)** and drag **Gamma** to **20**: every point grows its own little island.

C.label: C (strictness)
C.hint: Small = wide street, some mistakes allowed. Large = narrow, strict street.

gamma.label: Gamma (reach)
gamma.hint: How far each point's influence reaches. Large = very local, wiggly borders.

epochs.label: Epochs
epochs.hint: How many times every point is visited.

errors.oneClass: Add points of both classes: there is no street between one group and nothing.

sections.heading: What is a support vector machine?
sections.body:
A support vector machine (SVM) is a classifier that separates two classes with the **widest possible margin**. Among all boundaries that split the data, it picks the one that stays furthest from the closest points of both classes.

Those closest points are the **support vectors**. They alone define the boundary, which makes SVMs compact and, with few features, very robust.

sections.heading: Soft margins and C
sections.body: Perfectly separable data is rare. A **soft-margin** SVM allows some points inside the street or on the wrong side, and pays a penalty for each: the *hinge loss*. The parameter **C** sets the price. Small C: cheap violations, wide street, smoother boundary. Large C: expensive violations, narrow street that bends to fit the training points, with a risk of overfitting.

sections.heading: The kernel trick
sections.body:
An SVM only ever needs to know how similar two points are, measured by a dot product. Swap that dot product for a **kernel** function and the SVM behaves as if the data had been mapped into a richer space where a straight boundary works, without ever computing that space.

The popular **RBF** (Gaussian) kernel scores two points by how close they are. Its width `γ` matters: small γ gives smooth, wide curves; large γ lets every point influence only its own neighbourhood, which can overfit badly.

rows: Fails on rings, moons and other curved data

sections.heading: How it is trained here
sections.body: Classic SVM solvers use quadratic programming. This lesson uses **Pegasos**, a simple stochastic method: visit points in random order, and whenever one sits inside the street or on the wrong side, increase its weight `α`. The street that is drawn is the **average** of the street over all steps, a standard trick that makes Pegasos settle instead of jittering. The points with `α > 0` are the support vectors.

faq.q: Why is a wider margin better?
faq.a: New data is never exactly like the training data. A wide street leaves room for that noise, so new points are less likely to land on the wrong side. Learning theory backs this up: wider margins give better guarantees on unseen data.

The training points the boundary is built from: here, the ones that pushed at least once. At the exact SVM optimum they are precisely the points on the edges of the street or inside it; Pegasos gets close to that.

With a linear kernel they often give similar boundaries. Logistic regression gives probabilities; an SVM gives a margin and depends only on the hardest points. With kernels, SVMs draw curved boundaries that plain logistic regression can't.
Yes, especially on small and medium datasets with many features, such as text classification and bioinformatics. On huge datasets of images or text, neural networks have mostly taken over.

byHand.problem: A linear SVM has been trained on six points from two classes, +1 and −1. Its line is `w = (1, 1)`, `b = {b}`. Find the support vectors, measure the margin, work out the hinge loss and classify the new point `{qx}`.

steps.title: Score every point
steps.body: `f(x) = w · x + b` gives each point a signed score. Multiply it by the true label y: `y · f(x)` is positive when the point is on the correct side.

steps.title: Find the support vectors
steps.body: A trained SVM keeps `y · f(x) ≥ 1` for every point. Where it is exactly 1, the point touches the edge of the margin. These {supports} support vectors, {supportList}, are the only points that decide the line.

steps.title: Measure the margin
steps.body: The street between the two margin lines is `2 / ‖w‖ = {width}` wide. Training an SVM means making it as wide as possible.

steps.title: Hinge loss
steps.body: Each point pays `max(0, 1 − y · f(x))`. Every point here has `y · f(x) ≥ 1`, so the total loss is 0.

steps.title: Classify the new point
steps.body: The new point scores {score}. Its sign is the class.

byHand.answer: Support vectors {supportList}, a margin **{width}** wide, zero hinge loss, and `{qx}` belongs to class **{winner}**.
byHand.labNote: The Lab opens on the same six points (+1 is class B), but it trains the SVM itself instead of being given w and b. It ends close to the paper: `y · f(x)` is about 1 for {supportList} and about 2 for the others. Its supports counter also counts points that pushed the line early on, so it can show more than {supports}.
